newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's striking metalworkers stage mass protest.
newsitem.headline: Italy's striking metalworkers stage mass protest.

text.p: Striking Italian engineering and metal workers staged a mass demonstration in Rome on Friday to press their demands in an increasingly bitter pay dispute.

Trades union organisers said more than 150,000 workers, staging their second one-day strike in two months, converged on the city centre to protest over management's refusal to compensate in full for higher-than-expected inflation in the past contractual period.

Some 1,700 coaches and 25 special trains brought workers from around Italy to the Rome protest. Traffic in the centre was brought to a standstill as the army of strikers, many blowing whistles and waving brightly coloured banners, marched in a rally in the square of St John's Lateran.
An eight-hour strike was also held in September.
The metalwork sector forms the core of Italian industry and accounts for about 40 percent of total manufacturing output.
Among the companies affected by Friday's strike were car giant Fiat, technology group Olivetti and state shipbuilders Fincantieri.

Contracts for some 1.7 million metal and engineering workers expired at the end of June but employers and unions have failed to agree on new terms. The two sides last held talks back in September and no new meeting is planned.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government has said that if the employers' association, Federmeccanica, does not return to the negotiating table by November 28 it will intervene in the dispute and try to find a settlement.

Leaders of a number of government coalition parties, including Massimo D'Alema, the head of the largest force, the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), joined the strikers during their march through the capital.

In a bid to increase pressure on employers and support the metalworkers, Italy's unions earlier this week announced a national four-hour strike for December 13 across the industrial and transport sectors.
At the heart of the protracted dispute lies a battle over how to interpret a landmark 1993 labour pact.
The accord scrapped automatic index-linking of salaries on condition that management would make up any shortfall in wages if inflation ran above target.

But the wording of the deal was deliberately vague. Unions have interpreted it to mean that all the inflation overshoot should be covered. Management argue that only a part of lost earnings need be made up.

In cash terms, the unions want a gross 262,000 lire ($175) increase in their monthly pay packets, of which 97,000 is to cover the overrun in inflation between 1994 and 1996. Employers have offered 195,000 lire of which just 30,000 is for inflation.
"It is about time the employers respect the (1993) accord. This goes beyond wages, it's a matter of principles," PDS leader D'Alema said as he joined Friday's march.

While government parties have sympathised with unions, the employers have found an ally in the Bank of Italy which said last month that unions were not taking into account the recent falls in inflation and should therefore temper their demands.
Provisional data released on Thursday showed annual inflation in November running at 2.6 percent against six percent this time last year. $1 = 1,497 lire
